newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Macquarie hoses down buy-back talk.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Macquarie hoses down buy-back talk.

text.p: Investment bank Macquarie Bank Ltd moved on Wednesday to dampen growing speculation that it was planning a big share buy-back, saying any buy-back would be too small to bolster the share price.
Macquarie managing director Allan Moss told reporters after the group's annual meeting that Macquarie would consider its capital position later this year, but was happy to be strongly capitalised.
"Shareholders should not expect a large return in capital," Moss told reporters after the bank's annual meeting.
"There may not be any return in capital at all, but if there is one it will be modest," Moss said.

Macquarie is expecting its tier one capital adequacy ratio to be revised up to 13 percent from a current 10.7 percent when the Reserve Bank of Australia changes its guidelines on measuring market risk.
A ratio of 13 percent would be well above the four percent minimum set by the Reserve Bank and the nine percent level with which ratings agencies have said they would be comfortable.
But Moss said Macquarie liked being well capitalised as it was a growing company and already had strong return on equity.
"Having a very strong capital base does give us a lot commercial flexibility and of course the bank has been producing a very high return on equity of about 25 percent after tax," Moss said.
"It's not clear that we should be taking steps to reduce that capital ratio," he said.
"If there is one (a capital return), it will be modest because we've got a very fast-growing business here," he said.
"I do not think that the issue of a share buy-back will be a material factor for our stock."

Speculation on a capital return, probably through a share buy-back, has bubbled away since Macquarie's listing in July last year and as Macquarie itself has said it would look at its capital position as the Reserve Bank's guidelines were changed.
But the talk resurfaced this week when a newspaper said Macquarie would announce at the annual meeting that it was considering a buy-back.
The talk helped fire Macquarie's shares almost four percent higher this week to another all-time high of A$13.20 by the close on Wednesday.
The latest run took Macquarie's rally since its listing in July to over 60 percent from its initial price of A$6.95.
Macquarie's profit performance since listing has helped fuel the surge, with net profits rising 25.4 percent to A$116.94 million in the year to March 31, 1997.
Macquarie Chairman David Clarke also told the meeting the group's first quarter results to June 30 had been well ahead of the same quarter a year earlier.
Analysts agreed with Moss that Macquarie may need to keep its capital reserves well stocked if it was to continue expanding.
"They're an acquisitive bunch, so they're always going to need that capital," said one banking analyst.

Macquarie bought the Australian government's fleet leasing management company DASfleet for A$407.9 million in July and unsuccessfully bid to buy Axiom funds management from the New South Wales government earlier this year.
Analysts said however Macquarie's bull run of late may be at an end, with some baulking at the current price to earnings ratio on past earnings of about 17 to 18.
They said this was higher than for other investment banks around the world. U.S. investment banks J.P. Morgan and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter are both trading at p/e ratios of about 14.
They said a 17 to 18 p/e seemed high given investment banks could be seen as riskier propositions than some other stocks.
Investment banks tend to trade at reasonably conservative p/e ratios because their assets are employees able to arrange deals and trade rather than loans with steady income streams.
Investment bank earnings are also much harder to predict because they depended on market volumes and movements rather than interest margins.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
